p.text:
User wants ~350 words on how volcanoes form. No tools. Write factual prose, terse engineer style but essay. Keep ~350 words.

Content: mantle convection, decompression melting, three settings: divergent (mid-ocean ridges), convergent (subduction, flux melting from water), hotspots (mantle plumes). Magma generation, buoyancy, ascent, storage in chambers, fractional crystallization, gas exsolution, eruption style (viscosity, silica content), basalt vs andesite/rhyolite. Include numbers: mantle ~1300°C, decompression melting, ~10% melt, MORB, ring of fire 75%, etc.

Draft ~350.

Count: I'll aim 340-370.

Volcanoes are where molten rock reaches the surface. The central problem is that the mantle is hot but almost never molten: at roughly 1300 °C it sits below its solidus because pressure is high. Rock melts only when something shifts its pressure or composition, so volcanism marks the places where that happens.

Decompression melting dominates at divergent boundaries. Beneath mid-ocean ridges, convecting mantle rises, pressure falls, and the solidus drops faster than temperature does, so a few percent melt forms — perhaps 10–20% beneath fast ridges. That basalt feeds the global ridge system, which produces most of Earth's magma and builds new oceanic crust. Continental rifts such as East Africa work the same way, but through thick crust.

Subduction zones make the explosive volcanoes. Seawater locked into oceanic crust and sediment is driven off as the slab descends, and that water lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge — flux melting, not heating. The resulting andesitic magma is more silica-rich, more viscous, and more gas-laden than basalt, so it traps pressure and erupts violently. The Pacific Ring of Fire, hosting roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes, is this process.

Hotspots are the third setting: narrow upwellings, probably rooted near the core–mantle boundary, that melt as they rise. Because the plume is fixed relative to the moving plate, it leaves chains — Hawaii, Yellowstone, Iceland straddling a ridge.

Once melt forms, it ascends mainly because it is buoyant and because the surrounding rock deforms ductilely around it. Magma commonly stalls at neutral-buoyancy levels — the Moho, or shallow crustal chambers — where it cools, crystallizes, and differentiates; fractional removal of olivine and pyroxene drives residual melt toward silica-rich compositions. Dissolved water and CO₂ exsolve as pressure drops, expanding explosively near the surface.

Eruption style therefore follows viscosity and gas: low-silica basalt flows as lava (Kilauea, Iceland), while high-silica magma fragments into ash and pyroclastic flows (Pinatubo, Vesuvius). The chain is the same everywhere — melt generated by pressure or water, focused by buoyancy, modified in a chamber, released when gas wins.
